hints: Focus on where each C-Br bond can form a double bond, elimination needs a H on a neighbouring carbon.
Draw out 1,5-dibromopentane as $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ and check how many different neighbours each Br has.
Compare a symmetrical terminal dibromide with isomers where Br is in the middle, and ask which one forces the two new double bonds into only one set of positions.
walkthrough:
**Recall what double elimination does**

Each $\text{C-Br}$ loses $\text{Br}$ and a neighbouring $\text{C-H}$ loses $\text{H}$ to make a $\text{C=C}$ bond. Doing it twice from $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{Br}_2$ gives $\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$, which can be a diene, an alkyne or an allene.

$$2\text{NaOH} + \text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_8 + 2\text{NaBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Test 1,5-dibromopentane for choices**

Structure is $\text{BrCH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{Br}$. The Br on C1 can only lose H from C2, giving a C1=C2 bond. The Br on C5 can only lose H from C4, giving a C4=C5 bond.

$$\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{=CH-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH}_2$$

**See why this gives one product**

The molecule is symmetrical end to end, and there is no alternative neighbouring H for either Br. So only penta-1,4-diene can form.

$$\text{product} = \text{CH}_2\text{=CH-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH}_2 \text{ only}$$

**See why the others give more than one**

If Br is on C2, C3 or C4 it has two different neighbouring carbons to take H from, so the double bond can go in two directions. That creates isomeric dienes and also alkyne or allene options, for example penta-1,3-diene versus penta-1,4-diene from the 1,4-isomer, and pent-2-yne versus penta-2,3-diene from the 2,3-isomer.

options.A: Correct. Both Br atoms are terminal and each has only one adjacent carbon bearing H, C1 with C2 and C5 with C4. The molecule is symmetrical, so double dehydrobromination can only give $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH}_2$, penta-1,4-diene.
options.B: Wrong. 1,4-dibromopentane is $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3$. Br on C1 must give C1=C2, but Br on C4 can lose H from C3 to give C3=C4 or H from C5 to give C4=C5. This gives at least two dienes, penta-1,3-diene and penta-1,4-diene.
options.C: Wrong. 2,3-dibromopentane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, a vicinal dibromide. First elimination gives a bromopentene which can then eliminate in different directions to give pent-2-yne, $\text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and the allene penta-2,3-diene, plus the conjugated diene penta-1,3-diene. Several $\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$ isomers are possible.
options.D: Wrong. 2,4-dibromopentane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3$. Each Br has H neighbours on both sides, C1 or C3 for the C2-Br, and C3 or C5 for the C4-Br. Different combinations give different dienes such as penta-1,3-diene and penta-1,4-diene, and alkyne routes are also possible.
